summary: Privileged operations account used from an unusual host to enumerate secrets and create a new service token.
evidence: svc.ops used interactively from a workstation, but it normally runs only automated jobs
Secret enumeration and a new service token created
Account is used by the nightly backup and certificate-renewal jobs
investigation: Correlated with baseline: account had no interactive logins in 90 days
Confirmed with the platform team that the interactive use was not authorized
actions_taken: Per playbook default, the account was disabled
Nightly backup and certificate renewal failed overnight because they ran as this account
Analyst re-enabled the account after revoking sessions, removing the new token and rotating the account secret
outcome: Attacker access ended, but disabling the account caused a backup failure and an expired-certificate alert (about 9 hours of disruption).
analyst_feedback: For service/ops accounts with dependent automation, disabling the account was unnecessarily disruptive. Session revocation plus secret rotation plus removing the attacker's token was enough. Check dependent services before disabling.
lessons_learned: Before disabling an account, check what services and jobs depend on it
For privileged accounts with dependent automation prefer revoking sessions, removing attacker-created tokens and rotating the secret over disabling the account
detection_gaps: No alert for interactive logon of accounts that are normally non-interactive
